lesson.title: Slopes on Curves You Can't Solve for y
lesson.summary: Implicit differentiation lets you find dy/dx on curves like circles, even when the equation cannot be solved for y as a single function of x.
lesson.body:
Most of the curves you have differentiated so far came with y already isolated: y = x^2, y = sin(x), and so on. But plenty of important curves are written the other way around, as an equation relating x and y with no y by itself. The circle x^2 + y^2 = 25 is the simplest example. It is an implicit equation: for most values of x there are two y values that satisfy it, so the circle as a whole is not the graph of one function. Near the point (3, 4) you could solve for the upper branch, y = sqrt(25 - x^2), but for a messier equation like x^3 + y^3 = 6xy, there is no way to isolate y using ordinary algebra at all.

Even so, the circle clearly has a well-defined tangent line at (3, 4), and you should be able to find its slope. Implicit differentiation is the technique that gets you there without ever solving for y. The idea is to differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to x, term by term, treating y the whole time as an unspecified function of x. Wherever y appears, the chain rule applies, because you are really differentiating an inner function y(x) sitting inside whatever operation is being done to it. That produces a factor of dy/dx that you carry along and, at the end, solve for algebraically.

Here is the method on x^2 + y^2 = 25. Differentiate every term with respect to x: d/dx[x^2] + d/dx[y^2] = d/dx[25]. The first term is just 2x. The second term is 2y times dy/dx, by the chain rule, since y^2 is the square of a function of x. The right side is 0, since 25 is a constant. That gives 2x + 2y (dy/dx) = 0. Solving for dy/dx: dy/dx = -x/y. At the point (3, 4), dy/dx = -3/4.

You can check this against the explicit branch: y = sqrt(25 - x^2), so dy/dx = -x / sqrt(25 - x^2) = -x/y, which is exactly what implicit differentiation produced. The two methods agree whenever solving explicitly is even possible. The real payoff is that implicit differentiation keeps working when it is not, which is why it is worth learning as its own technique rather than a shortcut around algebra you could otherwise do by hand.
